content: A topic within programming that tends to inspire fairly strong opinions among coaches one way or the other is deloads. Some are fairly strongly against them, almost stating that you're just wasting a week of training. If you have 52 weeks in a year, why waste x amount of weeks deloading when you could be training? On the opposite end, including me, there are people very pro-deloads who utilize them in a very structured manner. Some being more reactive, while I am more structured, having planned deload weeks with the possibility of being reactive and needing the deload when necessary. Using deloads is very much a tool within training, not a punishment, nor a way to reduce progression or stop progression. Like some coaches, I think will kind of react towards them as a way of not training, so you're not going to progress as well. I think they help my lifters progress even more, so they're very much a tool we use. I'm going to go through the six reasons of why, with some of them being more of the reasons most people understand about deloads and kind of what they do physiologically. However, other ones being a bit more mental, and understanding that almost, I would say, maybe the bigger benefit of deloading is actually mental breaks for a lifter that almost helps more in the long term than the physiological effects.

So looking at the reasons why for a deload week, the first one, and probably the main one most people come to, is managing fatigue. Dissipating fatigue. We train for a certain period of time and get to a point where fatigue starts to overreach a little bit. So, we deload intensity and volume to kind of dissipate that and reset for the next training block. I look at that as a very important reason to deload. I think there's a lot more to deloading than just that, but very much so, when we get into a new training block, I want to have zero variables. I don't want to have fatigue variables that are carrying over from prior training blocks, which would mask what is occurring in this next training block, and I won’t know if it's working because something in the prior training block is still masking our ability to potentiate strength and show adaptations. In this next training block, deloading helps us to manage that fatigue and get us back to a certain baseline that's going to allow us to go into that next training block in a fresh state. The next reason that's pretty common, and that most people hear about, is kind of a re-sensitization to training, or re-sensitization—I can never say that word—to the stimulus presented. This means that we start to adapt to a stimulus, and we don't continue to progress from it, which is very true. However, I think maybe something that is used a bit is using a deload to re-sensitize the volume and intensity, and I don't think one week is really going to do that. I think if someone is used to higher volume or higher... Intensity, and we're trying to re-sensitize them to that. We're probably going to need a prolonged period of weeks, if not months, of lower volume and lower intensity for their body to kind of reacclimate to lower levels and to find a new baseline at that lower set point. The re-sensitization of a deload is less about re-sensitizing the volume and intensity, and more that we've produced the stimulus and adaptation we can from a training block. We cease to continue to progress from it, so we're going to manage fatigue. We're going to dissipate it so that we can restart a new block with a new set of stimuli and tools to be able to create progress in a fresh state when it comes to those first two points of managing fatigue. Re-synthesizing, I think a lot of times when people are doing that, they're thinking more of the muscles and the nervous system. Honestly, I don't think the muscles require a deload necessarily to allow our central nervous system to recover. I think the sense of thinking we're overreaching our nervous system tends to get overplayed a little bit. About three or four years ago, that was a big thing; they were literally just running our nervous system into the ground, so we had to deload for that. At least with me, I don't think I've ever had a lift or show start showing signs of truly nervous system fatigue because there are actually some pretty serious symptoms that go along with it. With that leading to the possibility of something like rhabdomyolysis, I've never had a lifter show any of those. I don't think we've ever gotten to the point where we truly run their nervous system into the ground to the point where they're needing a deload to survive and not go into these actual health concerns. What I think more is actually happening is, one, we are dissipating some fatigue. If we're going up to like a maximum recoverable volume, we're trying to bring our ability or our fatigue back down to ramp back up to that.

But more so, what probably needs recovery—that doesn't recover near as well as our muscles and our nervous system—are our tendons and ligaments. Something like a quad tendon. If someone's having continual issues with quad tendinopathy, we probably aren't going to see that dissipate and start to heal very well unless we do some type of change to volume and workload. That's pretty much injury management in a nutshell. I can make an entire video detailing exactly what we need to do when it comes to load management, to help with pain and flare-ups of injury or tendonitis in particular, where we get in our elbows or knees, anywhere it might be. We need to adjust workload. While a deload can be used almost kind of reactively if those things kind of spur up, I use them more proactively if we know at a certain point we started reaching that tipping point of fatigue, and if we go past. That we're going to start to kind of accumulate some possible workload-related issues. We're going to be having deloads scheduled regularly, so we know at that point, okay, that's where we're going to kind of push that point where we're starting to get fairly fatigued, and then we're going to deload to bring that back down. This way, we can be proactive to stay away from those issues of workload-related pain and flare-ups. With all that said, though, the physiological benefits of deloads—I honestly think the single biggest benefit I have with my lifters is the mental break that deloads provide. It's very common when I first start coaching someone and they aren't used to deloading, but they hate it. They absolutely hate it. Deloads, they get into the week and all they want to do is train, and they don't like having the deload. I actually don't mind that. For those who have been powerlifting for a while, eventually, the point that most powerlifters get to is that it's not always fun. There are some sessions we don't want to do; there are periods of time where we're burnt out. That happens in the longevity of the sport. We do three movements: we squat, we bench, and we deadlift. It tends to get boring over time, and a lot of times lifters have this kind of honeymoon period where they always enjoy training, and that eventually goes away. It is good to have breaks from training, mentally and even physically. If you don't want to break from training, I see a big benefit in missing training that week. Missing training in the sense of, like, I really want to train again, because what we see is this constant cycle of breaks mentally on a scheduled basis. The ability to miss training and to be excited, motivated, and focused to come back into a new training block shows a very high correlation to a lifter's progress and success. When it comes to fun, enjoyment, and motivation, those are big key success factors. Regularly scheduled deloads can help to keep those variables more consistent, versus seeing these long periods of time where we're burnt out and motivation is low. We can have these more... Regularly scheduled breaks allow for a mental break from training. This monotony of heavy training can really take its toll, and allowing that lifter to have a week to relax a little bit—maybe not have to be as mentally focused—is beneficial. Sometimes that focus can be stressful and anxiety levels can be high. It's important to have this mental refresher so they can return to training the next week and put more into it. That's where I see probably the biggest benefit. I've seen this time and time again with multiple lifters. After we've deloaded, we've tried maybe a wave loading approach, and within about five or six months, they... They come back to me and say, 'Can we go back to deloading?' I ask why. It has nothing to do with the training or the training progress. They're like, 'I just need a break.' I realize that, even though I didn't like deloads in the past, I now understand I really needed them because it just allowed me a week to kind of relax and have a mental break. So, that's what I see in the short term. If you've got one more powerlifting meet that you're ever going to do in your entire life and you need to put everything into those six months, maybe you don't deload. Maybe we need to maximize in a wave loading approach to increase the amount of productive training weeks we're doing in that six-month period. But if you're looking at... Most powerlifters who want to be successful need to consider that there's a long lifespan to be truly successful and competitive as a powerlifter, typically five to ten years. If we're looking at that span, we're going to be able to produce more consistent, efficient, and productive training by having regular scheduled deloads. This helps prevent burnout, reduces missed training, and creates excitement in training. The next point I'm going to get to is to allow life to happen. What I mean by allowing life to occur is that we are humans; we have jobs, we have families, we have final exams, we have vacations, and we have things that come up. Within the sense of deloading, reactive deloads are very beneficial for that. Being able to plan out a deload that can accommodate these life events is important. To line up with a vacation or, uh, an exam week, if you're a college student, you know you're just going to need to study, and you need to be able to prioritize other things in training. If we never deload and we never allow that option, it makes training very hard to fit in with life, which then eventually is sure to lead to training burnout. It's just going to happen because it creates this thing that our hobby, which most, I mean, 99% of people watching this video, is a hobby, not a profession. There are very few people that are going to make this a profession. There are very few people who are ever going to be competitive enough to even make this a profession in the sense of being an elite athlete, like Russ or Hy. Literally, some people live to train and make their living off of training and their business off of training.

Most of us do this as a hobby, and so it's not priority number one; it's priority number two, three, or four, below job, family, religion, anything like that. So we need to make sure it meshes in well with that. Deloads can really help to allow life to happen. In the sense of the argument of being reactive versus structured, because I do structure deloads and react if needed, some people say, 'Well, we don't need to ever structure it; we'll just be reactive when these things come up.' My argument to that is, yes, if things are coming up, we need to be reactive and plan for it, or we can just be proactive and allow the... An athlete should be able to know when they can plan for things. So, if an athlete knows that they always have a five-week training block with four weeks of training and one week of deloading, they can pretty much know when a deload is coming up. They can be able to plan for things, like scheduling more doctor's appointments, knowing that they probably have more time due to decreased training sessions. They might even plan a little mini trip and say, 'Hey Steve, can I do three sessions this week and combine two sessions versus four? I was going to go out of town Friday through Sunday, and I know it's a deload week, so would it be an issue if we combine those?' It allows them to plan ahead, and that just makes life easier. It makes life easier and less stressful, knowing that I'm going to have these weeks coming up that I can probably plan things for because I'm going to have more time. My training is going to be— I don't say not serious; we don't need to treat a deload like it's a week off. It's still a serious week, and we need to take training seriously. But at the same time, it does decrease the anxiety and stress of having to go in and lift really heavy weights and be very focused to be able to lift those weights in the best manner possible. So, we can take it with a bit more of a relaxed approach, and that allows people to have these mental breaks and be able to schedule life around training, which all leads back to longevity. Training for productive performance over a long period of time helps decrease mental burnout. The last thing, hopefully, that doesn't happen is injuries; however, they do occur. That's where we can be reactive with deloads. We need to be able to incorporate a deload week if we experience some type of pain flare-up or injury. While that is always an option, I regularly program structured deloads to try to be proactive and prevent that from ever being necessary. If we can use deloads to help manage fatigue a bit better, knowing that we reach a certain point in each training block where we start to kind of tip over the limit of what we can recover from, if we just plan deloads at that point, we can tend... To have longer periods of productive training without having injuries, now, powerlifting is a sport where injuries do occur, so that is going to happen eventually. But I just find that I can keep my athletes healthier by having these structured deload periods to be able to have a bit easier time managing fatigue, especially in the fact that I don't have anyone who trains to be a powerlifter professionally. There's life happening, so there are these fluctuations with how they're able to recover. Therefore, to be able to have those regularly scheduled deloads helps to make sure that we don't push past those during times of higher stress, higher workload, or higher personal life events going on. So, we've covered why the deload is important. Six reasons I kind of feel like deloads are needed within the structured way I actually programmed them. But also, a big question then is, when do I program these deloads if it's going to be in a structured manner, not reactive? A lot of that goes back to some of the things I talked about in my programming part one and programming part two in the series of volume and intensity, and I'll link those in the comments below. That was in the sense of time to peak. Very similar to kind of how Mike Tuchscherer does with his emerging strategies approach, which was kind of adopted from Bondarchuk. We tend to have a certain amount of times of exposure or certain weeks of training that we tend to peak our performance. What I typically see with my lifters is that we get to a certain point where strength continues to increase. The stimulus creates adaptations that produce progress, and then they seem to peak at a certain point. If we go one more week, they don't necessarily see this drop-off, which is what I think most people think is going to happen if they kind of go too far in their training or overreach, per se. It's more like we see this progression and then a little bit of a plateau. For example, in week four, they peak, and then we go to week five. In week five, what we see is more of a plateau; they don't really get stronger, per se. We see a similar level of performance. Performance, and then towards probably the end of week five, maybe you see a little regression. And then if we go to week six, we definitely start seeing some regression. So, I plan these deloads to be after that peak, because we know that coming into week five and six, if we're going to see plateau regression, we're no longer adapting and progressing with the stimulus of this training block. So, we're going to then deload instead, to be able to dissipate that fatigue and then go into a new training block with a new stimulus to adapt to. I keep using the word 'fresh state,' just meaning in a recovered state where we don't have this variable of fatigue masking our strength going into the next training block, typically. Within my system, and I always like to say 'my system' because every coach is a little bit different, and even if they're similar in some manner, their system may produce different results. Kind of what is the time to peak and when deloads should be structured, but I typically find most of my athletes are going to have somewhere between four to seven-week training blocks. So, if it's four weeks, that means three weeks of training and one week of deload, peaking sometime between three weeks and six weeks, with most people being in between. I would say the majority of people I coach are five-week training blocks or six-week training blocks, with those four weeks being a deload and then the fifth week being a deload, and we kind of find that. Structure, um, by being open-ended at first. And so, um, while eventually I like to be more structured with the deload process, when I first get a new lifter, I might write four weeks of training with a fifth week deload, but it's going to be very open-ended. We're going to keep going until we kind of see that plateau or regression. So maybe we go four weeks, and then we go into the fifth week and we see, uh, another continued spike in training, like we see more progress. But then we go into a sixth week and we see a plateau and a slight regression. Okay, noted. The fifth week, this lifter peaked on the first block we ever did together. That still doesn't mean that's their time to peak; that's only one training block, and every training block could be a little different. It's a bit different with the kind of stress we're inducing and when they're going to kind of reach that performance peak. So, we're gonna do another training block and maybe in this training block, they actually get to a six-week progression, and that was awesome. Then, we got to the seventh week, and we were still open-ended; we added a seventh week to that training but then we see a plateau regression. Okay, noted: in the first block, they peak in week five; in the second block, they peak in week six.

Then we get into a third training block. In this block, they peak in week five and regress in week six. Again, noted: peak in week five. The more data we accumulate and the longer I coach someone, the more we can say, 'Okay, 80 to 90 percent of the time, they're peaking in week.' Five, so we're probably just going to make that their standard block length. Then, just if a block is going really, really well and we don't have a timeline, we can be reactive and maybe add a week to it. What really helps, to be able to have that kind of time to peak and that knowledge of how long a training block should be, is that we start to have really consistent training, in the sense of being able to get the correct training stimulus, to be able to peak when we want, get the adaptations we want, and then deload when we need to, so we're not pushing past the recovery abilities. One of the big benefits of knowing this time to peak and their average training block length is using that to be able to set up and sense their. Meat prep and how they peak into a meet. If we know an athlete tends to peak on week four and we do a fifth week deload, we're going to try and set it up so that leading into the meet, we are running training blocks that fit into that schedule for multiple reasons. We'll really try to line that up. Let's say the final three blocks are really what we call kind of meat prep, and they're doing a 15-week meat prep, but we're 18 weeks out. I may very well do kind of like a little three-week mini block just to hold us over till we get to those 15 weeks, so we can line up their training to be within that five-week window. Each block, not only to make training the most productive and consistent, because we know they tend to peak on week. Four, and we'll deal with week five. But also, as we're peaking and tapering for a meet in that final training block, we know kind of how they respond in the sense of peaking on week four. Then, in week five, they start to kind of hit that point where, if we were to keep going, at the beginning of week five, they're plateaued. Well, then we know how we can slightly start tapering that week to get us back to peak performance in just a one-week span. If our training blocks are kind of a variable length and they're all over the place, it's going to be a bit harder to know exactly how to get them from that last week of training to taper into that Saturday, per se. But if we always run... Five weeks, and we know week four is the peak. Week five, we need to deload. Well, the deload now just turns into a taper, and it leads into the meet. It makes it much easier to be able to peak a lifter on meet day because we already have this consistent data set of exactly how they respond to training, block to block, when they're the strongest, and how we can kind of taper and deload off of that. Like I kind of alluded to, though, if a block is going great, especially if we don't have a timeline of a meet coming up, let's keep it rolling. Maybe we know this lifter always tends to peak week four, but we're in the middle of the offseason, and for some reason, training is going differently. Honestly, I saw this a lot this year with the situation. A lot of people weren't working as much, so we saw different life stressors. Maybe they were able to sleep and rest more; they had manual labor jobs they were no longer working for a period of time. We started to see different training data, different adaptations, and how they responded to training differently. If we didn't have a meet coming up, and if they normally peak in week four but they're doing really well and we're not seeing many fatigue markers indicating that they need to deload, we'll be reactive and start to add weeks after that. We should always be open-ended and reactive. I think that's where a lot of people start to kind of hate on or not understand the idea of structured delays. Deloads are structured, but they are still reactive at the same time. Unless we are in a timeline of a meat prep, per se, and we have a deadline for when we need to actually peak, we can always be very reactive with that deload and adjust as needed. Whether we need to shorten a training block because maybe life stress is really high and they’re not recovering very well, or they are recovering super well, we actually allow them to increase that stimulus if it’s going to keep producing adaptations and progress. So, if you usually watch my videos, you know I always like to go deep into the 'why,' so you have a really good understanding of the reasoning behind everything. I obviously went through the 'when' as well. Well, so we can understand when we need to deload, because the deload is a very important part of making it actually a productive and efficient tool that helps with improving our training. So, with that said, let's now get into the how. I'm going to kind of break down the general structure and template of deloads and understand that everything's kind of a range. I mean, every lifter is different, so I give more ranges of kind of between. Then I'm going to show you an example of one of my lifters' deloads, and then actually go through and program it while I'm doing a screen recording, so you can see me going through exactly how I'm going to program that. Afterwards, we'll finish off with kind of the caveats here of understanding if there is a range and there are different lifters. How do we understand how to adjust that based off of individual response? So, let's get into it. So, here we've got our deload set, rep, and intensity structure. Within the way I deload, we have a volume drop and an intensity drop. With some people, how they deload might just be a volume drop while keeping the intensity up. I'm not a huge fan of that, just for the reason that I don't think tendons and ligaments do very well with not dropping intensity. That's just from experience; it's not from any scientific data or anything. I've just found that when people don't drop intensity, tendons and ligaments don't respond well. We tend to respond well if we're not dropping intensity a little bit along with volume. Then some people, they actually keep, uh, they drop intensity, but then they keep volume the same. Again, I think that could possibly work; that's basically more like a wave loading approach. Um, so when I'm talking in a deload manner, I'm talking about some type of structure of a volume and an intensity drop. As we're going through this, I have set up here kind of the different categories of exercise. We have squat, bench press, and deadlift—so the competition movements and their variants. It's like a pause squat or something like that. Um, compound pressing accessory, something like a dumbbell bench press, isolation pec, or shoulder. Accessories: something like a cable fly or a side lateral raise, compound quad accessory, something that might be more like a belt squat, a reverse lunge, a leg press, a compound hinge accessory, something like a dumbbell RDL or a hyperextension, isolation quad or hamstring accessory movement, so something like a leg extension or a hamstring curl. Pull accessory: so any rowing or pull-down movements. Upper back accessory: like rear flies or face pulls. Tricep accessory: like a tricep extension. Bicep accessory: like bicep curls. And then lastly, just because I'm a big fan of blood flow restriction training and I like including it, I included blood flow restriction as part of how we're going to go through this. So within this, I have set... Repetition and intensity, and kind of how we're going to fluctuate that, because all three of these are variables that we can manipulate based on each individual exercise here. So with squat, I have here that I'm going to drop one set per workout. So what does that mean? Well, let's say the lifter is squatting twice a week, and they squat five sets on day one and five sets on day two. That means on day one I'm going to have them squat four total sets, and on day two I'm going to have them squat four total sets. So one set drop per workout. For bench press, we're not going to drop any sets, because I'll kind of get around to this. I mean, obviously, each lift is independent of each other, and bench press tends to not need to be deloaded as much. Dropping sets and dropping repetitions both affect volume, so we can do one or the other, or both, to either increase or decrease how much volume we're dropping. So, with bench press, if we have five sets on one day, I'm not going to drop any of those. On deadlift, we're going to drop one set per workout, just like squat. Then, really going down all of these movements, we're gonna drop one set per exercise. So, if they were doing two sets of three sets of ten on dumbbell bench press, they're gonna do two sets of ten. The only one I don't drop on with the accessories is blood flow restriction, and that's just because if you've ever done blood flow restriction, I typically do it in a four-set manner. If you drop a set, you really don't get much. You can benefit from it, so you kind of have to keep these sets and the reps the same. I'll describe that a little more in a second. So, like I said, sets and repetitions can both affect volume. For squats, we're also going to drop one rep, so if they were doing five sets of five, I would now have them do four sets of four—one set dropped and one rep dropped. For bench press, if they're doing five sets of five, we're not dropping a set; we're just dropping a rep. So they're going to do five sets of four, which is a little bit less of a volume drop. And then for deadlifts, for most people, deadlifts tend to create the highest fatigue, especially conventional deadlifts. Deadlifts tend to carry a lot of fatigue from deadlifting. That could be a whole video on kind of why that is. And I mean, arguably one of the biggest reasons is usually just lifting the most weight on the deadlift, so there's going to be the most systematic fatigue carried over from it. So, we could drop anywhere between one to two reps per set. Instead of doing four sets of four, just dropping one rep, we might go with four sets of three, just dependent on each lifter and kind of the extent they need to deload. For all of the accessories, mainly because they're just not going to be as fatiguing. I mean, that's the reason why we use accessory movements—to allow those to be added for the hypertrophy benefits and to fill in volume gaps without creating as much fatigue as a squat or bench press. For the deadlift, we're not going to drop any reps. So, if we were doing three sets of 10 on the dumbbell bench press, we're going to drop one set. We're going to keep the reps the same and do two sets of ten, so that we still have the adequate repetitions there and we don't do too much of a volume drop. That goes for all the exercises. Then we get into intensity. So, that's how we kind of compound things. With the squat, I'll tend to do anywhere between a 7.5% to 12.5% drop from the prior week. We have to understand that if week four was our peak week and that was our heaviest week, we are doing about a 7.5% to 12.5% drop from that. I can tell. With some of my lifters, especially on bench press, their deload week is actually almost heavier than their week one sometimes. But we are doing a rep drop. If we're doing a one-rep drop or a set drop, we're still decreasing total volume.

However, by dropping a rep on top of intensity, we're also decreasing relative intensity because that weight is now relative to one rep less per set. So, somewhere between 7.5 to 12.5 based on the lifter's needs, which we'll cover in a little bit. Bench press is not nearly as fatiguing, probably only five to ten percent. There are some people I barely deload their bench press because if we deload it too much, they detraining very easily. So, I usually do a much lower deload on the bench press. Intensity drops when it comes to the bench press, and as I already mentioned, the deadlift tends to fatigue the highest. So again, depending on the lifter, somewhere probably between a 10 to 15% intensity drop. And then, as we're going through accessory movements, accessory modes are all the same. A dumbbell bench press is not the same as a cable fly. So on a dumbbell bench press, I'm probably going to do about a 5 to 10% intensity drop, which is usually going to be maybe 5 to 10 pounds. If they're using 80-pound dumbbells, they might be going down to 75-pound dumbbells this week. For an isolation pec or shoulder accessory, I suggest more like a 3 to 5% drop to a 1 RPE. So if it was programmed at an 8 RPE, now I'm... Programming it at a 7 RPE for a compound quad or a hinge accessory, very much like a squat or deadlift, tends to be more fatiguing than a pressing movement. So, I usually have these deload a bit more with the accessory movements, such as a belt squat or a lunge, somewhere between 7.5 to 15, dependent on the lifter and maybe the intensity that weight was even programmed at in the first place. For an isolation quad and hamstring accessory, I'm going to go one RPE for a pull accessory. I keep saying one RPE because one RPE equates to about three percent. So, I'm really... for most of these, I'm just dropping one RPE versus saying drop three percent because it's much easier for a lifter to be able to. To kind of conceptualize dropping one RPE for the tricep accessory, somewhere around one to two RPE, depending on the intensity I had it at, and then for blood flow restriction, like I said, if they were doing four sets of 12 with blood flow restriction, I'm just going to keep that volume the same. We're just going to do an intensity drop because for those who aren't familiar with blood flow restriction, you're using maybe 30 to 40% of the weight you normally use. It's fairly low impact, so we're just going to make it a little bit easier by dropping a couple of RPEs. We're not going to complete failure by that fourth set, so that's the general structure I'm looking at for the framework of the set repetition and intensity drop I have within. The deload week and how that kind of plays out is looking here. I have the total volume reduction kind of calculated here, so we can see the intensity drop depending on each lift. It's going to be somewhere between 5 to 15 percent for the intensity average drop on the week. For volume for squat, what's going to happen is it's going to play out to around 50 to 60 percent volume of the previous week, so about a 40 to 50 percent drop. For bench press, it's about 70 to 80 percent of the volume of the previous week, and for deadlift, about 45 to 55 percent. So, the example I'm actually going to show you is their total volume from week five: about 27,000 on squat, about 23,000 on bench press, and about 17,500 on deadlift. A deload week, so I think this is about 58 percent. This is about 58 percent. We'll actually just calculate real quick, and I'll show you. About 58 percent of the bench was about 75 percent of the prior week's volume, and deadlift was about 48 percent of the prior week's volume. So again, a general framework for the extent we're going to deload, when it comes to the volume reduction during a deload week, is to be able to dissipate fatigue and be able to go into the next training block fully recovered.
